# 5xx

*Status code* · also written 5xx errors · server errors · server error

The class of HTTP status codes for server errors; Google slows crawling when it sees them and drops URLs that keep returning them.

**Glossary** (*HTTP status code classes*): 1xx informational, 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client error and 5xx server error. Each class affects crawling differently, and 429 is the 4xx code that tells Google to slow down instead of saying there is nothing at the URL.

Narrative: the topic [Crawl errors](../topics/crawl-errors.md) tells the story; this card lists what links to it.

12 claims mention it: 4 from Google's documentation, 4 shown or said at the event (1 confirmed by Google docs, 3 consistent with Google docs), 4 the author's analysis. A card is a map: cite the claim ids, with the citation given after each claim.

## Google's documentation

Documented in: [How HTTP status codes affect Google's crawlers](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/troubleshooting/http-status-codes), [Troubleshoot Google Search crawling errors](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/troubleshoot-crawling-errors).

- [`D1-C126`](../sessions/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) Docs: Google treats network timeouts, connection resets and DNS errors like 5xx server errors: crawling slows down immediately, and already indexed URLs that stay unreachable are removed from Google's index within days. `[D1-C126, docs, Google, https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/troubleshooting/dns-network-errors]`
- [`D1-C071`](../sessions/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) Docs: 5xx and 429 responses prompt Google's crawlers to slow down temporarily. Already indexed URLs are preserved in the index for a while but eventually dropped. `[D1-C071, docs, Google, https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/troubleshooting/http-status-codes]`
- [`D1-C074`](../sessions/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) Docs: If robots.txt returns a 5xx error, Google stops crawling the site for the first 12 hours, then uses the cached copy for up to 30 days. `[D1-C074, docs, Google, https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/robots-txt/robots-txt-spec]`
- [`D1-C460`](../sessions/D1-S12-q-a.md) Docs: Chrome's Lighthouse documentation lists an llms.txt audit among its agentic browsing audits: it flags a server error when llms.txt is fetched and marks the audit not applicable when the file is missing, because providing the file is optional for now. `[D1-C460, docs, Chrome for Developers, https://developer.chrome.com/docs/lighthouse/agentic-browsing/llms-txt]`

## Shown or said at the event

Not in Google's documentation first: present those as said at Search Central Live, never as documented policy.

- [`D1-C354`](../sessions/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) Stage, Day 1, confirmed by Google docs: Google slows crawling when a site returns 5xx errors, because a 5xx usually means the server, and often the whole site, cannot serve requests, and Google does not want to break the site. `[D1-C354, stage, Cherry Prommawin, Day 1]`
- [`D1-C345`](../sessions/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) Stage, Day 1, consistent with Google docs: HTTP status codes fall into five classes, 1xx informational, 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client error and 5xx server error, and each class affects crawling differently. `[D1-C345, stage, Cherry Prommawin, Day 1]`
- [`D1-C092`](../sessions/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) Slide, Day 1, consistent with Google docs: Hostload is driven by changes in connect time, changes in time to first byte, and HTTP 429 or 5xx status codes. If these increase, hostload is adjusted and crawling slows down. `[D1-C092, slide, Google, Day 1]`
- [`D1-C099`](../sessions/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) Slide, Day 1, consistent with Google docs: Three things burn crawl budget: server errors unrelated to server load, useless pages and resources, and infinite URL spaces. `[D1-C099, slide, Google, Day 1]`

## The author's analysis

- [`D1-C386`](../sessions/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) Analysis: The stage point that 4xx responses do not affect crawl budget matches Google's documentation that 4xx codes have no effect on crawl rate (D1-C072), with one exception: 429 Too Many Requests counts as a server error and slows crawling like a 5xx (D1-C071, D1-C092). `[D1-C386, analysis, Ibrahim Anjro]`
- [`D2-C210`](../sessions/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) Analysis: An API or CDN on its own host needs its own robots.txt check: a blanket Disallow there, or a robots.txt that returns 5xx errors, can stop Google fetching the data a page renders from. `[D2-C210, analysis, Ibrahim Anjro]`
- [`D2-C708`](../sessions/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) Analysis: The help page explains 'Discovered – currently not indexed' by expected server overload (capacity), while on stage it was explained as Google not wanting the URL yet (demand); the crawl budget guide covers both, so first rule out slow responses and server errors, then treat the status as a quality and demand problem. `[D2-C708, analysis, Ibrahim Anjro]`
- [`D3-C621`](../sessions/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) Analysis: Spoken and slide figures for capacity increases differ (one to three weeks, up to a month, versus 1-2 weeks typical and 1-3 weeks in recovery), but the lesson is the same: a burst of 5xx errors cuts crawling within hours and recovery takes weeks, so keep servers stable before launches and migrations. `[D3-C621, analysis, Ibrahim Anjro]`
